title: 1  Scarcity, Choice and the Frontier
text:
1.1 Definitions
Consider an economy with 6,000 hours of labor and no more. An hour that goes into a bicycle is an hour that cannot go into a jacket, and wanting more of both goods does not add a single hour to the supply.
Suppose a bicycle takes 6 hours of labor to make and a jacket takes 2. The opportunity cost of a bicycle is then 3 jackets, because that is what the 6 hours would otherwise have made.
Consider an airline about to depart with one unsold seat. If a standby passenger offers $300 for it, the airline takes the money, because $300 serves its interests better than a seat that flies empty.
Take the economy with 6,000 hours of labor, where a bicycle takes 6 hours and a jacket takes 2. Every hour is used on the frontier, so \(6B + 2J = 6000\), which rearranges to \(J = 3000 - 3B\). The frontier runs from 3,000 jackets and no bicycles to 1,000 bicycles and no jackets.
We can see all three on the frontier \(J = 3000 - 3B\). The combination of 400 bicycles and 1,800 jackets is on the boundary, so it is efficient, and the slope of \(-3\) says that one more bicycle costs 3 jackets. No point beyond the line can be reached with the hours available.
Suppose the economy makes 400 bicycles and wants 100 more. At 3 jackets each, the extra bicycles cost 300 jackets, and jackets fall from 1,800 to 1,500.
Suppose the frontier for food and clothing is \(C = 50 - 0.02F^{2}\). The first 10 units of food cost 2 units of clothing, and the last 10 units cost 18.
On the frontier \(C = 50 - 0.02F^{2}\), an economy that grows 40 units of food can make 18 units of clothing. So 40 food with 18 clothing is efficient, and 40 food with 24 clothing is out of reach. With 40 food and fewer than 18 clothing, the economy is inside its frontier.
Go back to the point with 40 units of food and 24 of clothing, which the frontier \(C = 50 - 0.02F^{2}\) does not allow. Suppose that after growth the same 40 units of food permit about 32 units of clothing. The point has not moved, but it is now inside the frontier.
The claim that a higher minimum wage reduces teenage employment is positive, because we can look at the data and the data may show it to be wrong. The claim that the government should raise the minimum wage is normative.

title: 1  Scarcity, Choice and the Frontier
text:
Scarcity. Scarcity means that resources are finite relative to what people want. Because resources are finite, there are competing claims on them. Scarcity means constraint. We cannot have more than there is, even if we want more.



Opportunity cost. An opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative that is forgone. It is measured in units of the thing that is given up, not necessarily in money. It is the only cost concept that appears in every model in this book.



Rationality. A rational agent is one who makes consistent choices given the objectives they have. They take the best action that serves their interests given all of the information and constraints that they face. Rational agents are in effect goal oriented.



Production possibility frontier. Given its technology, a production possibility frontier shows the maximum combinations of two goods that an economy can produce when all of its resources are used fully and efficiently.



One picture, three ideas. The frontier brings together three ideas: scarcity, efficiency and opportunity cost. Scarcity shows up as the existence of a boundary, because some combinations are simply not available. Productive efficiency means being on the boundary rather than inside it. Opportunity cost is the slope of the boundary, leaving aside its minus sign. This is not an analogy. The size of the slope and the opportunity cost are one and the same number.



Constant opportunity cost gives a straight line. The equation \(J = 3000 - 3B\) has a slope of \(-3\), so each extra bicycle costs three jackets. That number is not something read off the graph. It comes straight from the labor data: \[\frac{6\ \text{hours per bicycle}}{2\ \text{hours per jacket}} = 3
    \ \frac{\text{jackets}}{\text{bicycle}} .\] That is because the six hours that go into a bicycle could otherwise have made three jackets. Every hour is equally productive at either task, so the cost is the same at every point on the frontier. A constant slope gives a straight line.



Increasing opportunity cost. A straight-line frontier assumes that every unit of the resource is equally suited to making both goods. In practice, resources are usually specialized. So as production shifts toward one good, the expanding sector has to draw in resources that are less and less suited to it. Each additional unit therefore costs more than the one before. When the slope gets steeper, the opportunity cost increases and the frontier is bowed.



Three kinds of point. A point on the frontier is productively efficient: you cannot get more of one good without giving up some of the other. A point inside the frontier is feasible but inefficient, because the same resources could produce more of both goods. A point outside the frontier is out of reach with current resources and technology.



Economic growth. Economic growth is an outward shift of the frontier. It enlarges the set of combinations that the economy can attain.



Positive and normative statements. A positive statement is a claim about how the world is, and in principle evidence can confirm or refute it. A normative statement is a claim about how the world ought to be. It rests on values as well as on facts.

title: 1  Scarcity, Choice and the Frontier
text:
1.2 Worked examples

The cost of a year of college. An example illustrates the idea of an opportunity cost. Consider the cost of a year of college. Tuition and fees are the explicit costs. Let’s suppose these are $32,000. Forgone earnings are the implicit costs. For example, a year’s worth of full-time work might earn $38,000. Therefore the opportunity cost of the year is $70,000.
Notice that room and board don’t come into it, because whether you’re at college or working full time, you still have to pay for room and board. Only the difference between what they cost at college and what they would cost otherwise is part of the opportunity cost.


The concert ticket. As before, an example illustrates. Suppose you buy a concert ticket that costs $150. It is non-refundable, and you can’t sell it on to anybody else. On the night of the concert, it’s raining and you would rather stay in. No matter what, the $150 is gone. The reasonable comparison now is between the happiness, or what economists call utility, that you get from going to the concert and the utility you get from spending the evening at home. The price is now irrelevant.
A standard error is to suppose that not going to the concert now wastes $150. However, that is the wrong way to think about things. The $150 was already spent when the ticket was bought. The decision after the cost is sunk depends totally on the utility of the two options, staying at home or going to the concert. There is nothing you can do about the cost. Worrying about it, and thinking it should be part of the decision, is known as the sunk cost fallacy.


The empty seat. Once again, a simple example might illustrate this. Suppose an aircraft has 200 seats and is about to depart with one unsold seat. The average cost per passenger is $500. Now suppose there is a standby passenger, and that person offers $300. From the airline’s point of view, is the seat worth selling? The answer is yes, sell. Why? The flight is going to go regardless, so the crew, fuel, aircraft and everything else are already committed. The marginal cost of carrying one more passenger is near zero. It is a drink and a little more fuel, perhaps $5. So the marginal benefit to the airline is $300 against a marginal cost of a trivial $5.
The $500 average includes costs that do not change when the passenger boards. It answers a different question, and it is the wrong number when deciding what is the rational thing to do.

title: 2  Gains from Trade
text:
2.1 Definitions
Consider Smith’s pin workshop, where ten men who divide the work between them make upwards of forty-eight thousand pins in a day. A man who makes only pins must get his food, clothing and shelter from others, so he specializes and he exchanges.
Suppose a unit of cloth takes 100 hours of labor in England and 90 in Portugal, and a unit of wine takes 120 hours in England and 80 in Portugal. Portugal needs fewer hours for both goods, so it has the absolute advantage in both.
A unit of wine costs Portugal 0.89 units of cloth and costs England 1.20, so Portugal has the comparative advantage in wine. A unit of cloth costs England 0.83 units of wine and costs Portugal 1.125, so England has the comparative advantage in cloth, even though it needs more hours than Portugal for both goods.
Suppose England puts 1,800 hours into each good. It then makes 18 units of cloth and 15 of wine, and under autarky that is exactly what it consumes.
Here England has 3,600 hours of labor and Portugal 2,880, and the autarky figures suppose that each country splits its hours equally between the two goods. So world output rises by two units of cloth and three of wine, and no hour of labor has been added.
Suppose 17 units of wine trade for 17 units of cloth, so that \(p = 1\). That price is above Portugal’s cost of 0.89 units of cloth and below England’s cost of 1.20, so both countries accept it.
After trade England consumes 19 units of cloth and 17 of wine. Its own frontier allows only 15.6 units of cloth at 17 units of wine, so England is consuming a bundle that it could not have produced.

title: 2  Gains from Trade
text:
Specialization and exchange. Agents concentrate their production on a narrow range of goods and get the rest by exchange. Nobody produces everything they consume.



Absolute advantage. Producing a good with fewer inputs than another producer does. It is a direct comparison of productivities.



Comparative advantage. Producing a good at a lower opportunity cost than another producer does.



Autarky. The absence of trade. A country consumes precisely what it produces, so its production frontier is also its consumption frontier.



Specialization raises world output. Now suppose all of each country’s labor moves into the good in which that country holds the comparative advantage. England then produces \(3600/100 = 36\) units of cloth and no wine. Portugal produces \(2880/80 = 36\) units of wine and no cloth. World output is now 36 units of cloth and 36 of wine, against 34 and 33 under autarky.



Terms of trade. The rate at which the two goods exchange once trade opens. Let \(p\) be the price of one unit of wine in units of cloth. There is no money in the model, so a price is a ratio between goods.
Portugal sells wine, and it will not accept less than its own cost of producing wine. That requires \(p > \tfrac{8}{9} \approx 0.89\). England buys wine, and it will not pay more than its own cost of producing wine, which requires \(p < 1.20\). Both conditions hold only within \[\tfrac{8}{9} < p < 1.20 .\]



Consumption beyond the frontier. With trade, a country’s consumption point may lie outside its own production frontier. Production is still bounded by the frontier. Consumption is bounded by what the country produces together with what that production can be exchanged for.

Ricardo states these requirements as the labor of a given number of men for one year. Here they are read as hours. That changes nothing, because only the ratios between the four figures do any work.

Ricardo gave labor requirements but did not say how much labor each country had. Labor requirements fix the slope of a frontier but not its position, so the two endowments must be supplied here: England 3,600 hours and Portugal 2,880. title: 3  Supply and Demand
text:
3.1 Definitions
In the coffee market that runs through this chapter, quantity is measured in thousands of cups per week, price in dollars per cup, and demand is
\[
Q^{d} = 70 - 10P .
\tag{3.1}\]
Raise the price from $3 to $4 with nothing else changed, and the quantity demanded falls from 40 thousand cups to 30 thousand.
Suppose the market has two buyers, and at a price of $3 Ama demands 24 thousand cups while Ben demands 16 thousand. The market quantity demanded at $3 is then \(24 + 16 = 40\) thousand cups, and the two buyers face the same price, so no prices are added.
Supply in the coffee market is \(Q^{s} = 10P - 10\). At $3 sellers offer 20 thousand cups a week and at $4 they offer 30 thousand, because the higher price makes the extra output worth producing.
In the coffee market, quantity demanded and quantity supplied are both 30 thousand cups a week at a price of $4, so $4 is the equilibrium price. At $3 buyers want 40 thousand cups and sellers offer only 20 thousand, which means that $3 does not clear the market.
Suppose demand for coffee goes up by 20 at every price while supply stays where it was. The equilibrium moves from $4 and 30 thousand cups to $5 and 40 thousand cups, and the method reports those two points without saying how the market got from the first to the second.

title: 3  Supply and Demand
text:
The law of demand. Other things equal, when the price of a good goes up, the quantity demanded of that good goes down.





Market demand. The horizontal sum of the individual demand curves. At each price, add up the quantities that each buyer demands.



The law of supply. Other things equal, when the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied of that good rises.



Market equilibrium. The price and quantity at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. At that price the market clears. Every buyer who is willing to pay it finds a seller, and every seller who is willing to accept it finds a buyer.



Comparative statics. Comparing the equilibrium before an event with the equilibrium after it. The method compares two resting points and says nothing about the path between them or the time it takes.

  \qquad \text{surplus} = 20 .\] Unsold stock piles up, and sellers cut their prices to clear it. \(Q^{s}\) falls, \(Q^{d}\) rises, and once again the market ends up at $4.

Case 1, demand increases. Suppose a study reports that coffee is good for your health. Demand goes up by 20 at every price, so the intercept moves from 70 to 90. Supply stays where it was. \[90 - 10P = 10P - 10 \;\Longrightarrow\; 100 = 20P \;\Longrightarrow\; P^{*} = 5 ,\] \[Q^{*} = 10(5) - 10 = 40 .\] Check it through demand: \(90 - 50 = 40\). The price moves $4 \(\to\) $5 and the quantity moves 30 \(\to\) 40, so both rise.

Figure 3.4 shows the shift.

Case 2, supply decreases. Now suppose a frost destroys part of the crop. Supply falls by 20 at every price, so its intercept moves from \(-10\) to \(-30\). This time demand stays put. \[70 - 10P = 10P - 30 \;\Longrightarrow\; 100 = 20P \;\Longrightarrow\; P^{*} = 5 ,\] \[Q^{*} = 10(5) - 30 = 20 .\] Again, check through demand: \(70 - 50 = 20\). The price moves $4 \(\to\) $5, but the quantity moves 30 \(\to\) 20. This time they go in opposite directions.

Figure 3.5 shows the shift.






Figure 3.5: Case 2. Supply shifts left and the equilibrium moves up along a fixed demand curve. The price rises and the quantity falls.

title: 4  Elasticity
text:
4.1 Definitions
For example, a slope of 10 in the coffee market means thousands of cups per dollar, so it cannot be put beside a slope from the housing market. An elasticity of 1.80 can be compared across markets, because the units have gone.
On the coffee curve, a price change of 22.2 percent goes with a quantity change of 40 percent, so \(|E_{d}| = 40.0/22.2 = 1.80\). The law of demand makes the sign negative every time, and for that reason we report the absolute value.
For example, when coffee is $4 the elasticity is 1.33, so demand at that price is elastic. At $2 it is 0.40, and demand is inelastic.
The coffee curve is \(Q^{d} = 70 - 10P\), so \(b = 10\). At a price of $4.50 the quantity is 25, and the point elasticity is \(10 \times 4.50/25 = 1.80\).
Here \(\bar{P}\) and \(\bar{Q}\) are the averages of the two prices and of the two quantities. Take the coffee prices of $5 and $4, where the quantities are 20 and 30. The averages are 4.50 and 25, so the arc elasticity is \(10 \times 4.50/25 = 1.80\).
On the diagram, the first case is a vertical demand curve, with \(|E_{d}| = 0\). The second is a horizontal one, where \(|E_{d}| \to \infty\).
The estimated elasticities show the determinants at work. Eggs, at 0.1, have no close substitute and take a small share of the budget, while restaurant meals, at 2.3, have substitutes everywhere.
For example, at the coffee equilibrium the price is $4 and the quantity is 30 thousand cups, so \(TR = 4 \times 30 = \$120\) thousand per week.
Suppose 100 units sell at $10, and the price rises by 20 percent, to $12. If \(|E_{d}| = 2\), quantity falls to 60 and revenue falls from $1,000 to $720. If \(|E_{d}| = 0.5\), quantity falls only to 90, and revenue rises to $1,080.
Suppose a bakery supplies 3,000 loaves a week at $3 a loaf, and 5,000 loaves at $4. By the midpoint method, quantity changes by 50 percent and price by 28.6 percent, so \(E_{s} = 1.75\) and supply is elastic.
On the diagram, the supply of beachfront land is a vertical line, with the same quantity at every price. The other extreme is a horizontal line at the going price.
For example, take a $1 tax in a market where \(|E_{d}| = 0.43\) and \(E_{s} = 1.71\). Buyers pay $6.80, up from $6.00, and sellers keep $5.80, so buyers bear 80 cents of every dollar of tax and sellers bear 20 cents.

title: 4  Elasticity
text:
Elasticity. The percentage change in one variable divided by the percentage change in another variable. Because the numerator and the denominator are both percentages, the units cancel and the ratio is a pure number. It has no cups in it, no dollars and no bushels.



Price elasticity of demand. \[E_{d} = \frac{\%\,\Delta Q^{d}}{\%\,\Delta P} .\] Quantity goes in the numerator and price goes in the denominator. If you swap them, you are answering a different question.

Point elasticity of demand. The price elasticity of demand, evaluated at a single point on a straight-line demand curve \(Q^{d} = a - bP\), \[|E_{d}| = \left| \frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta P} \cdot \frac{P}{Q} \right|
          = b\,\frac{P}{Q} .\] Along a straight line, \(\Delta Q / \Delta P = -b\) at every point, and for a price change of any size. That means the measure is exact.



Arc elasticity of demand. The price elasticity of demand, evaluated at the averages of two points on a straight-line demand curve \(Q^{d} = a - bP\), \[|E_{d}| = \left| \frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta P} \cdot \frac{\bar{P}}{\bar{Q}} \right|
          = b\,\frac{\bar{P}}{\bar{Q}} .\]



The two extremes. Perfectly inelastic, the vertical case. For example, a transplant patient will buy the prescribed dose of anti-rejection medication at very nearly any price. There is no substitute for the medication, and there is no option of taking less. So a change in price moves the quantity bought very little, and demand comes close to the vertical case.
Perfectly elastic, the horizontal case. Consider one wheat farmer among thousands, selling wheat identical to everyone else’s. If the farmer charges a cent above the going price, every buyer goes elsewhere. If the farmer charges a cent below it, the farmer is simply giving money away.



The five determinants.

Close substitutes. Butter’s price rises and buyers switch to margarine; eggs have no stand-in, so egg buyers stay. More substitutes mean more elasticity.
How the market is drawn. Food has no substitute and its demand is inelastic. One bakery’s sourdough loaf has a substitute in every other bakery and its demand is highly elastic. The narrower the market, the more elastic the demand.
Necessity or luxury. A doctor’s visit happens at almost any price; a sailboat does not.
Share of income. Rent doubling rearranges a life; salt doubling goes unnoticed. A bigger budget share makes demand more elastic.
Time to adjust. Gasoline jumps and this month the driving to work continues. Over years come a smaller car, a carpool, a move closer in.




Total revenue. The total amount that buyers pay and that sellers receive, \(TR = P \times Q\). On the diagram, total revenue is a rectangle whose height is the price and whose width is the quantity. So revenue is not an extra concept attached to supply and demand. It is an area that has been inside the picture all along.



Elasticity and total revenue. Suppose the price rises. The price effect is that each unit now sells for more, and that pushes \(TR\) up. The quantity effect is that fewer units are sold, and that pushes \(TR\) down.
Which of the effects wins? The elasticity settles that, because it measures exactly what is in dispute: whether quantity moves proportionately more or less than price.

When demand is elastic, it is the quantity effect that wins. When demand is inelastic, it is the price effect.



Price elasticity of supply. \[E_{s} = \frac{\%\,\Delta Q^{s}}{\%\,\Delta P} .\] Because supply slopes upward, both changes have the same sign, and so \(E_{s}\) comes out positive on its own, with no need for an absolute value. The vocabulary carries over unchanged. Supply is elastic above one, unit elastic at one and inelastic below one, and the same two extremes sit at the ends.



The hard limit. Some quantities are fixed by nature rather than by cost. No price, however high, will create more coastline. So the physical supply of beachfront land is perfectly inelastic, \(E_{s} = 0\). This is the one constraint that no amount of time will relax.
At the other extreme is \(E_{s} \to \infty\), which is a horizontal supply curve. At the going price, the quantity supplied responds without limit.



Tax incidence. Who actually bears the burden of a tax, as opposed to who is legally required to hand the money over. The person who writes the check is not necessarily the person who pays.

title: 5  Price Controls and Taxes
text:
5.1 Definitions
Take the coffee market, where \(Q^{d} = 70 - 10P\) and \(Q^{s} = 10P - 10\), which clears at a price of $4 with 30 thousand cups sold a week. A ceiling of $5 sits above that price and forbids nothing that was going to happen anyway, whereas a ceiling of $3 sits below it, and so $3 becomes the price that holds.
In the same coffee market, a floor of $5 sits above the $4 equilibrium, so it forbids the price the market was heading toward and it binds. A minimum wage works in the same way: where the labor market would clear at $8 an hour, a floor of $10 is binding.

title: 5  Price Controls and Taxes
text:
Price ceiling. A legal maximum on the price at which a good can be sold. The standard example is rent control, and there the motive is usually to protect buyers.



Price floor. A legal minimum on the price at which a good can be sold. The standard example here is the minimum wage, and the motive is usually to protect sellers.

title: 5  Price Controls and Taxes
text:
5.2 Worked examples

A binding ceiling at $3. In this case the ceiling binds, so the price is $3. The demand and supply schedules both stay as they were. The only thing that has been fixed is the price. \[Q^{d} = 70 - 10(3) = 40 , \qquad Q^{s} = 10(3) - 10 = 20 .\] So the shortage is 20 thousand cups per week. The quantity actually traded is also 20 thousand, because a cup that was never produced cannot be bought by anybody.
Ordinarily, a shortage like this would push the price back up to $4, and the shortage would close itself. But the ceiling forbids that price. So the mechanism that would have closed the gap no longer operates, and the shortage persists for as long as the ceiling is in place.
Figure 5.1 shows this market.







Figure 5.1: A binding ceiling at $3. The shortage is a horizontal distance: a gap between two quantities at one price, never a gap between two prices.




A binding floor at $5. \[Q^{d} = 70 - 10(5) = 20 , \qquad Q^{s} = 10(5) - 10 = 40 .\] The surplus is 20 thousand cups that sellers would supply but buyers will not take, whereas the ceiling produced unmet demand. The price cannot fall back to $4 and clear it away, so the surplus persists.
Figure 5.2 shows this market.







Figure 5.2: A binding floor at $5. A control line above equilibrium always leaves supply exceeding demand; one below it always leaves demand exceeding supply.

A floor at $10. Ten is above eight, so this floor is binding. \[L^{d} = 150 - 10(10) = 50 , \qquad L^{s} = 10(10) - 10 = 90 .\] The surplus is 40 thousand workers. A surplus of labor is what we call unemployment.
That 40 thousand is really made up of two things, which are equal here by construction. Employment fell from 70 to 50, so 20 thousand jobs were destroyed. At the same time, labor supply rose from 70 to 90, so 20 thousand more were drawn into the search. They came because $10 an hour is worth working for, whereas $8 was not. There are two ways to check it. Demand at the buyers’ price gives \(70 - 10(4.50) = 25\). The original supply curve at the sellers’ price gives \(10(3.50) - 10 = 25\). So the buyers’ price goes into the demand equation, and the sellers’ price goes into the original supply equation.

title: 6  Market Efficiency
text:
6.1 Definitions
For example, Maya would hand over at most $6.00 for a cup of coffee, and Ben would hand over at most $2.00. So at a price of $4.00, Maya buys and Ben does not.
Consider Maya’s morning, cup by cup. Her first cup is worth $6.00 to her, her second $4.50, her third $3.00 and her fourth $1.50, so at a price of $4.00 she buys two cups and then stops.
Suppose the price of a cup is $3.50. Maya would have paid $6.00, so her consumer surplus is \(6.00 - 3.50 = \$2.50\), while Priya, who would have paid exactly $3.50, gains $0.
For example, it costs Rosa $1.50 to supply a cup from her cart. At a price of $3.00, her producer surplus on that cup is \(3.00 - 1.50 = \$1.50\).
The worked examples below use a coffee market with demand \(Q^{d} = 70 - 10P\) and supply \(Q^{s} = 10P - 10\), which clears at a price of $4 with 30 thousand cups traded a week. In that market, consumer surplus is $45,000 and producer surplus is $45,000, so total surplus is \(45 + 45 = \$90{,}000\) per week.
In the coffee market, the efficient quantity is 30 thousand cups. At 20 thousand, the marginal cup is worth $5.00 to a buyer and costs $3.00 to make, so stopping there gives up value, and at 40 thousand it is worth $3.00 and costs $5.00, so the last cups destroy value.
For example, suppose a trade affects people other than its own buyer and seller. Then the value and the cost that the market acts on are not the full value and the full cost, and the quantity it trades is not the one that maximizes total surplus.

title: 6  Market Efficiency
text:
Willingness to pay. Willingness to pay is the most that a buyer would hand over for one unit of a good. If the seller charges even one cent more than that, the buyer does not trade.



Diminishing marginal utility. Each additional unit that a buyer consumes adds less satisfaction than the unit before it. So if we hold fixed what a dollar is worth to the buyer, the dollar value that the buyer places on each successive unit falls.



Consumer surplus. Consumer surplus is what a buyer would have paid minus what the buyer actually pays, \(\text{CS} = \text{WTP} - P\). It measures the buyer’s gain from the trade, in dollars.



Producer surplus. Producer surplus is what a seller is paid minus the seller’s cost, \(\text{PS} = P - \text{cost}\). On a diagram, it is the area above the supply curve and below the price, out to the quantity traded.



Total surplus. Total surplus is consumer surplus plus producer surplus. It is the whole gain that the market creates for the people who take part in it.



Efficiency. An allocation is efficient when it maximizes total surplus. In an efficient allocation, no change in who buys, who sells or how much is traded can create more value.



Market failure. Market failure is a situation in which the equilibrium of an unregulated market does not maximize total surplus.

title: 6  Market Efficiency
text:
6.2 Worked examples

Consumer surplus in the coffee market. At \(P^{*} = \$4\) the market trades \(Q^{*} = 30\) thousand cups. The demand curve starts at $7. That is the choke price, and it is also the value of the first cup. From there the curve runs down to $4, which is the value of the marginal cup at 30 thousand. So the region is a triangle. Its base is 30, and its height is \(7 - 4 = 3\): \[\text{CS} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 30 \times (7 - 4)
            = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 30 \times 3
            = 45 .\] So buyers gain $45,000 a week in total.

Figure 6.1 shows this triangle.






Figure 6.1: Consumer surplus at the equilibrium price. The shaded triangle lies below the demand curve and above $4, out to 30 thousand cups.




A price of $5. Now suppose the price rises to $5. At that price, quantity demanded falls to 20 thousand cups, and \[\text{CS} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 20 \times (7 - 5) = 20 ,\] so consumer surplus falls from $45,000 to $20,000. That is a loss of $25,000, and the loss has two parts. First, buyers pay $1 more on each of the 20 thousand cups that they still buy, and that comes to $20,000. Second, some buyers drop out and no longer buy. They lose the surplus they were earning on 10 thousand cups, which were worth between $4 and $5 to them. That lost surplus is a small triangle, \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 1 = \$5{,}000\). Add the two parts together, and we are back at $25,000.

Figure 6.2 shows the two parts of the loss.






Figure 6.2: A rise in the price from $4 to $5 reduces consumer surplus in two parts: a rectangle paid by buyers who continue to buy, and a triangle of surplus on trades that no longer occur.




Producer surplus in the coffee market. At \(P^{*} = \$4\) the supply curve starts at $1. That is the minimum supply price, the cost of the cheapest cup to make. The curve then runs up to $4, which is the cost of the marginal cup at 30 thousand: \[\text{PS} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 30 \times (4 - 1)
            = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 30 \times 3
            = 45 .\] So sellers gain $45,000 a week. As on the buyers’ side, the marginal cup earns exactly zero surplus, because at the margin the price equals the cost.

Below 30 thousand, the gap between value and cost is positive. Each further cup is worth more than it costs, so stopping early gives up gains that were there to be had. Above 30 thousand, the gap is negative. Each further cup costs more than it is worth, so producing it destroys value. At 30 thousand, the gap is zero. That is the quantity at which total surplus reaches its maximum. It is also the quantity at which the market settles, without anyone giving instructions.


A cap on the quantity. Suppose a licensing rule permits only 20 thousand cups per week, and the price is free to adjust. The trades between 20 and 30 thousand cups were creating value. Over that whole range, marginal value was above marginal cost, so the gap was positive. The licensing rule now prohibits those trades.
The surplus that is lost is a triangle. At 20 thousand cups, the gap between marginal value and marginal cost is $2.00. The gap then shrinks to zero at 30 thousand. So the loss is \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 2 = \$10{,}000\), and total surplus falls from $90,000 to $80,000.
There is a second, independent route to the same figure. On the \(Q\)th cup, the gain from trade is the difference between marginal value and marginal cost, \[\frac{70 - Q}{10} - \frac{Q + 10}{10} = \frac{60 - 2Q}{10} = 6 - 0.2Q ,\] which is $6.00 on the first cup and $2.00 on the twenty-thousandth. The gain falls along a straight line, so take the average over that range: \((6.00 + 2.00)/2 = \$4.00\). Then multiply the average by the number of cups, and \(4.00 \times 20 = \$80{,}000\).
The two routes give the same answer. Each of them is an exact computation of the same quantity. So if they disagreed, that would point to a slip in the arithmetic, rather than to a disagreement about the economics.

title: 7  Externalities
text:
7.1 Definitions
Consider the market for firewood in a valley town, where \(Q^{d} = 100 - 10P\) and \(Q^{s} = 10P - 20\), and \(Q\) is measured in hundreds of bundles per week. Every bundle that is burned sends smoke onto households that bought no wood, and we suppose that the smoke from each bundle does $2.00 of harm to them.
For example, at 4,000 bundles a week the marginal bundle of firewood has a private cost of $6.00. Add the $2.00 of harm from its smoke, and the social cost of that bundle is $8.00.
The firewood market trades 4,000 bundles a week, but the quantity that maximizes total surplus is 3,000. Each of the 1,000 bundles in between costs society more than it is worth to its buyer, and the value destroyed adds up to $1,000 per week.
Suppose the firewood seller has to pay the $2.00 of harm on every bundle. Then the seller of bundle 4,000 faces the full $8.00 that the bundle costs society, and not only the $6.00 that it costs to produce.
A corrective tax is also called a Pigovian tax, and for firewood it is $2.00 a bundle. With the tax in place, buyers pay $7 a bundle, sellers keep $5, and the quantity falls from 4,000 bundles a week to 3,000.
Consider a bike-share system in a congested city, where \(Q^{d} = 80 - 10P\) and \(Q^{s} = 10P - 20\), and \(Q\) is measured in hundreds of rides per day, and suppose each ride is worth $2.00 to the drivers who are still on the road. At 3,000 rides a day the marginal ride is worth $5.00 to its rider, so its social value is $7.00.
Suppose two factories each discharge 80 tons a month into the same river, and the town wants the total brought down to 100 tons. The town issues 100 permits, and a factory that cuts a ton can sell the permit this frees up to the other factory.
For example, suppose live music is worth $400 a week to a café, and costs the bookshop next door $600 a week in lost sales. The bookshop can offer the café $500 to keep quiet, and that leaves each of them $100 better off, even though the law gives the café the right to play.

title: 7  Externalities
text:
Externality. A cost or a benefit, arising from producing or consuming a good, that lands on someone who is not a party to the decision. That someone is called a bystander. The bystander neither pays for the effect nor is paid for it, through any price or contract.



Social cost. The private cost plus the external cost. Put another way, it is what one more unit costs society once the bystanders are included.



Deadweight loss. The total surplus that is lost to an inefficient outcome, most often because the quantity traded is not the quantity that maximizes total surplus. It is value destroyed either by trading too much or by trading too little, and nobody collects it.



Internalizing an externality. Changing incentives so that the parties to a trade face the full social cost of that trade, or its full social value.



Corrective tax. A tax on each unit, set equal to the external cost that the unit imposes. It lifts the curve that sellers respond to by exactly the amount by which that curve fell short of social cost.



Social value. Private value, meaning the buyer’s willingness to pay, plus the external benefit. In other words, it is what one more unit is worth to society when the bystanders are counted.



Tradable pollution permits. Each permit allows its holder to discharge one unit. The number of permits issued is equal to the cap, and firms may buy and sell them.



Coase theorem. If the affected parties can bargain at no cost, they will reach the efficient outcome by themselves, whichever side the law favors to begin with.

Two factories on one river. Northside Mill and Harbor Chemical each discharge 80 tons a month into the same river, for a total of 160 tons. The town wants to bring that total down to 100 tons, which means cutting 60 tons between them. Cutting one ton costs the Mill $50, and it costs Harbor $150.
Suppose the rule requires each firm to cut 30 tons: \[\text{Mill: } 30 \times \$50 = \$1{,}500 , \qquad
  \text{Harbor: } 30 \times \$150 = \$4{,}500 ,\] for a total of $6,000 a month, and the target is met exactly.


The same cap through permits. The town issues 100 permits, 50 to each firm. Because there are only two firms, the price has to be negotiated between them, and any price between the Mill’s $50 and Harbor’s $150 suits both. They agree on $100.
The Mill can cut a ton for $50, and each permit it holds is worth $100. So if it cuts a ton and sells the permit that this frees up, the Mill nets $50. It cuts 60 tons, which is as many as Harbor will buy permits for. That costs \(60 \times \$50 = \$3{,}000\). The Mill is then emitting 20 tons and holding 30 spare permits, which it sells for \(30 \times \$100 = \$3{,}000\). So its net cost is $0.
Harbor cuts nothing, because cutting costs it $150 a ton while a permit costs $100. So it buys the Mill’s 30 permits for $3,000 and goes on emitting 80 tons.
Emissions total \(20 + 80 = 100\) tons, the same cap that the rule achieved. The only real resources used up are the Mill’s $3,000 of abatement. The $3,000 in permit payments is a transfer between the two firms. It buys no cleanup and destroys nothing. So the true cost is $3,000, compared with $6,000 under the rule.

Figure 7.3: What 60 tons of abatement costs under each instrument. The rule buys 30 of the tons at Harbor’s $150, and the permit market moves all 60 to the Mill at $50.




Two plants and a 40-ton target. Plant A can cut a ton for $80, and plant B for $30. Each plant emits 50 tons, and the state wants the total brought down to 60, so 40 tons must be cut.
Under a uniform rule, each plant cuts 20 tons, and that costs \(20 \times \$80 + 20 \times \$30 = \$1{,}600 + \$600 = \$2{,}200\).
Now suppose the state issues 60 permits instead, 30 to each plant, and the two plants agree on a price of $55. Plant B cuts all 40 tons, which costs \(40 \times \$30 = \$1{,}200\), and emits 10. It sells 20 permits for \(20 \times \$55 = \$1{,}100\), so its net cost is $100. Plant A cuts nothing and buys those 20 permits for $1,100. Emissions are \(10 + 50 = 60\), and society’s real abatement bill is B’s $1,200.
For both firms to prefer trading to the rule, the permit price must lie between the two firms’ own costs. Take plant A first. It buys 20 permits, instead of cutting 20 tons at a cost of $1,600, when \(20p < 1{,}600\), that is, when \(p < \$80\). Now take plant B. It cuts 40 and sells 20, at a net cost of \(1{,}200 - 20p\). It prefers that to the $600 it would pay under the rule when \(1{,}200 - 20p < 600\), that is, when \(p > \$30\). Both conditions hold when \[\$30 < p < \$80 .\] At a price of $80, plant A is indifferent between buying a permit and cutting the ton itself. At $30, it is plant B that is indifferent. So each end of the range is one firm’s own cost per ton.


A café, a bookshop and a Friday night. Live music on Fridays at Café Solana is worth $400 a week to the café. The noise carries into Harriman Books next door, and it costs the bookshop $600 a week in lost evening sales. Under the law, the café has the right to play.
Quiet is worth $600 and the music is worth $400. So quiet creates more value, and yet the law allows the outcome that creates less.
Suppose the bookshop offers the café $500 to keep Fridays quiet. The café compares that $500 with the $400 value it places on the music, and it accepts. The bookshop avoids $600 of losses and pays $500, so it is $100 better off. The café gives up $400 of value and receives $500, so it too is $100 better off. No regulator is involved, and yet the efficient outcome is reached, because the bystander stopped being a bystander by making an offer.

title: 8  Public Goods and Common Resources
text:
8.1 Definitions
A burrito is excludable, because if there is no payment there is no burrito. Street lighting is not excludable, since the light that falls on a paying pedestrian falls just as much on the next one.
A fish, once landed, cannot be landed a second time, so fish are rival in use. A streamed show is not rival, because one person’s viewing of it takes nothing away from anyone else’s.
The mosquito treatment program at Alder Pond is a public good. A licensed crew treats the pond for $2,500 a season, and all 120 households around it get the benefit whether they pay or not.
The neighborhood association asks each of the 120 households around Alder Pond for $25. Take a household that values a mosquito-free season at $50. If it keeps its $25 and the program runs, it is a free rider, because the treatment reaches its yard either way.
For the Alder Pond program, the total benefit to the 120 households is $3,300 a season and the total cost is $2,500. The benefit is larger by $800, so the program is worth doing.
Birch Lake is a common resource, because it is open to anyone with a boat. Catch per boat is \(1200 - 100\,b\) dollars of fish a day, where \(b\) is the number of boats on the water, so every boat already fishing loses $100 of catch when one more boat launches.
A boat-day on Birch Lake costs $400. The fifth boat lands $700 of fish, so it launches, but $400 of that catch is fish the other four boats would have landed anyway.
On Birch Lake a fleet of four boats earns a net $1,600 a day. Under open access eight boats launch, each one catches $400 against a cost of $400, and the net is $0.

title: 8  Public Goods and Common Resources
text:
Excludable. A good is excludable if a supplier can stop people who have not paid for it from using it.



Rival in use. A good is rival in use if one person’s use of a unit reduces what is left over for everybody else.



Public good. A good that is neither excludable nor rival. Nobody can be kept out, and a single supply serves everybody at once.



Free rider. A person who enjoys the benefit of a good without paying for it.



Cost-benefit analysis. Comparing the total benefit of a project, to everyone it affects, with its total cost, in order to decide whether the project is worth doing.



Common resource. A good that is rival in use but not excludable. Anyone may take from it, and every taking leaves less for the rest.



The tragedy of the commons. A user weighs the full private gain against the fraction of the true cost that lands on that user. Take any use whose full cost to everyone exceeds its gain, but whose private share of that cost does not. That use gets undertaken, and those are exactly the uses that should not happen.



Rent dissipation. The rent of a resource is the value that the resource itself generates over and above the cost of working it. Under open access, entry continues until every user exactly breaks even. A fleet in which every boat breaks even generates no net value at all. The rent is fully dissipated.

title: 9  Public Choice
text:
9.1 Definitions
Take the coffee market of Chapter 6 under a cap of 20 thousand cups a week. Buyers pay $5 a cup and the twenty-thousandth cup costs $3 to produce, so the rent is \((5 - 3) \times 20 = 40\), or $40,000 a week. It is the rectangle in Figure 9.1.
Suppose 10 sellers hold the licenses, with $78,000 a year at stake each, and 10,000 buyers purchase the coffee, with $130 a year at stake each. So a holder can gain by paying for a campaign to keep the cap, and a buyer cannot gain by paying for one to remove it, even though the buyers lose more as a group.
Consider a buyer with $130 a year at stake and a 1 in 100,000 chance of casting the decisive vote. The expected benefit of learning about the cap is $0.0013, and learning takes an hour valued at $20, so the buyer stays uninformed.
Suppose the council will issue 10 licenses, each a right to sell 2,000 cups a week and each worth $4,000 a week. If applicants spend the full $40,000 on lawyers and consultants to win them, the cap costs society $50,000 a week and not $10,000, as Figure 9.2 shows.
A licensing board could raise the cap to 30 thousand cups. Each holder would then lose $1,500 a week and each buyer would gain $2.50, so the arguments the board hears about the size of the cap come mainly from the holders.

title: 9  Public Choice
text:
Rent created by a restriction. The price minus the marginal cost at the restricted quantity, multiplied by that quantity. The rent is paid to whoever holds the right to sell, and it exists only because the restriction exists.



Collective action problem. The failure of a group of people to act in their common interest.



Rational ignorance. Choosing to stay uninformed about a policy because the expected benefit of learning about it is less than the cost of learning.



Rent-seeking. Spending real resources to obtain a transfer that a policy has created. The spending determines who gets the transfer, and it adds nothing to output.



Regulatory capture. The decisions of a regulator come to serve the industry that it regulates.

title: 10  Production and Costs
text:
10.1 Definitions
Consider an engineer who works as an independent consultant and bills $280,000 in a year. Once all of her costs are counted, they come to $210,000, so her profit is $70,000.
The engineer pays $30,000 in office rent and $20,000 for equipment, and both are explicit costs. The $150,000 salary she gave up to work for herself is an implicit cost, and so is the $10,000 of interest that her $200,000 of savings no longer earns at 5 percent.
On revenue of $280,000, the engineer’s accounting profit is \(280{,}000 - 50{,}000 = \$230{,}000\), and her economic profit is \(280{,}000 - 210{,}000 = \$70{,}000\). The gap between the two is $160,000, which is exactly her implicit costs, \(150{,}000 + 10{,}000\).
A food truck can change everything about its operation in perhaps six weeks, while a nuclear plant may need a decade. So the long run is not a number of months. It is however long the fixed input takes to become a matter of choice.
Take a firm that assembles electronic components, with its machines and floor space fixed and \(L\) workers per shift. Its production function is
\[
Q = 24L - L^{2} , \qquad 0 \le L \le 12 ,
\tag{10.1}\]
with \(Q\) measured in components per shift, so 3 workers produce \(72 - 9 = 63\) components.
The assembler makes 63 components with 3 workers and 80 with 4. The marginal product of the fourth worker is therefore \(80 - 63 = 17\) components.
The assembler’s first worker adds 23 components and the twelfth adds only 1. The twelfth worker is no less capable than the first. She adds less because the same machines are now shared among 12 people.
The assembler pays $50 for a worker-shift. The first worker adds 23 components, so each of them costs \(50/23 = \$2.17\). The ninth worker adds 7, so each of those costs \(50/7 = \$7.14\), although the wage has not changed.
The workshop here builds oak chairs, and its daily total cost in dollars for \(Q\) chairs is \(TC = 100 + 60Q - 12Q^{2} + Q^{3}\). At 6 chairs a day total cost is $244, of which $100 is fixed and \(244 - 100 = \$144\) is variable.
At 6 chairs a day the workshop has \(AFC = 100/6 = \$16.67\), \(AVC = 144/6 = \$24.00\) and \(ATC = 244/6 = \$40.67\). We can check the identity on these numbers, since \(16.67 + 24.00 = 40.67\).
The workshop’s total cost is $225 at 5 chairs and $244 at 6, so the marginal cost of the sixth chair is \(244 - 225 = \$19\). None of the fixed $100 is in that figure, because the $100 was owed anyway.
The workshop’s seventh chair costs $31 and joins an average of $40.67, so the average falls to $39.29. The eighth chair costs $49, which is more than $39.29, and the average rises to $40.50.
For the chair workshop the efficient scale is 7 chairs a day, where average total cost is $39.29. This is not necessarily the output the workshop should choose, because profit depends on price as well as on cost.
Suppose a firm can build a small, a medium or a large plant. The small plant is the cheapest per unit when orders are thin and the large plant when volume is high, and the long-run curve takes whichever is lowest at each output.
Adam Smith’s pin factory of ten workers split the making of a pin into distinct operations. It produced tens of thousands of pins a day, where a lone artisan performing every step himself could scarcely make 20. That is an economy of scale. Diseconomies arrive later, when management layers multiply and the cost of coordination rises faster than output.

title: 10  Production and Costs
text:
Profit. Total revenue minus total cost, written \(\pi = TR - TC\), where \(TR = P \times Q\).



Explicit and implicit costs. Explicit costs are input costs that require a direct money payment, such as wages, rent, materials and the interest on a loan. Implicit costs are input costs that involve no money payment. They are the value of what the owner gives up, for example the salary not earned elsewhere and the interest the invested savings could have earned.



Accounting profit and economic profit. Accounting profit is total revenue minus explicit costs. Economic profit is total revenue minus all opportunity costs, both explicit and implicit.



Short run and long run. In the short run at least one input is fixed. For example, the firm can hire workers at short notice, but it cannot build a bigger factory at short notice. In the long run all inputs are variable, including the size of the factory.



Production function. The relationship between the inputs a firm uses and the output it produces, written here as \(Q = f(L)\).





Marginal product. The additional output produced by one more unit of an input, holding the other inputs fixed: \(MP = \Delta Q / \Delta L\).



Diminishing marginal product. As more and more of a variable input is added, with the other inputs held fixed, the marginal product of that input eventually falls.



Marginal cost is the wage divided by marginal product. Hiring one more worker costs the wage \(w\) and yields \(MP\) extra units of output, so each of those units costs \[MC = \frac{w}{MP} .\]



Fixed and variable costs. Fixed costs, \(FC\), do not vary with output, and they are owed even at \(Q = 0\). For the workshop, \(FC = 100\). Variable costs, \(VC\), vary with output. In this case \(VC = 60Q - 12Q^{2} + Q^{3}\). Every dollar of total cost is one or the other, so \(TC = FC + VC\).



The three average costs. Average fixed cost is \(AFC = FC/Q\), which is the fixed bill spread over the units produced. Average variable cost is \(AVC = VC/Q\), the variable bill per unit. Average total cost is \(ATC = TC/Q\), which is what the typical unit costs. Since \(TC = FC + VC\), dividing through by \(Q\) gives \(ATC = AFC + AVC\).



Marginal cost. The increase in total cost that comes from producing one more unit, \(MC = \Delta TC / \Delta Q\).



The pulling principle. The cost of each new unit is a new mark entering the average. If \(MC < ATC\), the new unit is cheap and pulls the average down. If \(MC > ATC\), the newcomer is expensive and drags the average up. If \(MC = ATC\), the average stands still.
As long as \(MC\) lies below \(ATC\), average total cost is falling. Once \(MC\) lies above \(ATC\), average total cost is rising. A quantity that falls and then rises has its minimum at the changeover. In a table the changeover falls between two rows, where \(MC\) passes from below \(ATC\) to above it. On smooth cost curves it is the point where \(MC = ATC\) exactly. Marginal cost therefore crosses average total cost at the minimum of average total cost.



Efficient scale. The quantity of output at which average total cost is lowest.



Long-run average cost. The lowest average total cost attainable at each level of output when the firm is free to choose its factory. Geometrically, it is the lower envelope of the short-run average total cost curves.



Economies and diseconomies of scale. Economies of scale occur where \(LRAC\) falls as output rises. Constant returns to scale occur where \(LRAC\) is flat. Diseconomies of scale occur where \(LRAC\) rises as output rises.

title: 11  Firms in Competitive Markets
text:
11.1 Definitions
The running example of this chapter sits in the top row. It is a maker of standardized electronic connectors, one of 120 identical firms, with total cost \(TC = 144 + 36q - 8q^{2} + q^{3}\) dollars a day, where \(q\) is one firm’s output and \(Q\) is the output of the whole market.
The connector market meets all three conditions. One supplier’s output is indistinguishable from another’s, no plant is big enough to matter on its own, and anyone may open a plant or close one.
Suppose the market price of a connector is $48. A firm that charges $49 loses every buyer to a rival, and a firm that charges $47 wins no extra sales, because it could already sell its whole output at $48. It simply hands a dollar to each buyer.
At $48 the connector firm’s revenue is \(TR = 48q\), so a seventh connector raises revenue from $288 to $336, and \(MR = 336 - 288 = \$48\). Marginal revenue equals the price because the firm never has to cut its price to sell more.
At $48 the sixth connector costs $39 to make and the seventh costs $59. So the firm makes the sixth, skips the seventh, and produces \(q^{*} = 6\).
At a price of $71 the firm produces 7, where \(ATC\) is $49.57. The rectangle is \(71 - 49.57 = 21.43\) high and 7 wide, so its area is $150 (Figure 11.1).
The connector firm supplies nothing at $15, 5 at $31, 6 at $48 and 7 at $71. At exactly $20, the minimum of its average variable cost, it is indifferent between producing 4 and producing nothing.
A connector firm that exits stops paying its fixed bill of $144 a day. A firm that merely shuts down keeps paying it and waits for the price to recover.
At a price of $31 the connector firm makes 5 and loses $94 a day, but $31 is above its average variable cost of $21 at that output, so it operates today. It also arranges to leave when the lease expires, because $31 does not cover all of its costs.
When connector demand rises, the price first spikes to $71 and then falls back to $48.20 as 58 new firms enter, so the industry grows from 120 firms to 178 (Stages 1 to 3 below).
The three conditions are one point, because marginal cost crosses average total cost at its minimum (Chapter 10). For the connector firm the point is \(q = 6\) at $48.
Suppose entrants to a farming market face a minimum \(ATC\) of $48 at \(q = 6\), and a few incumbent farms on unusually good land face $40. The price settles at $48, set by the marginal entrant, so a good-land farm earns at least \((48 - 40) \times 6 = \$48\) a day, and entry cannot compete it away because entrants cannot copy the land.
Suppose connector plants need a specialized alloy in limited supply. A wave of entry bids up the alloy’s price, every firm’s cost curves shift up, and a bigger market needs a permanently higher price.

The fewer the sellers and the more distinctive the product, the more each firm can typically say about its own price.



Competitive market. A market with many buyers and many sellers, in which the goods are identical across sellers and there is free entry and exit.



Price taker. A buyer or seller who takes the market price as given and cannot influence it.



Average and marginal revenue. Average revenue is the revenue per unit sold, \(AR = TR/q\). Marginal revenue is the change in total revenue when the firm sells one more unit, \(MR = \Delta TR\).



The output rule. If \(MR > MC\), the next unit brings in more than it costs, so making it raises profit, and the firm expands. If \(MR < MC\), the last unit cost more than it brought in, so cutting it raises profit, and the firm cuts back. So profit is greatest at the last unit whose \(MR\) still covers its \(MC\). When output can be varied in fractions, that point is exactly where \(MR = MC\). The rule holds for every firm that maximizes profit. For a price taker, \(MR = P\), so the rule becomes \(P = MC\).



Constructing the profit rectangle. First find the output, where the price line meets marginal cost. Then read average total cost at that same output, not at its minimum. The vertical gap between the price line and the \(ATC\) curve is profit per unit. The rectangle runs from zero to \(q^{*}\), with its top at the price line and its bottom at \(ATC\), and its area is profit.



The firm’s short-run supply curve. The firm’s short-run supply curve is its marginal cost curve above average variable cost, and zero below it. In whole units the curve rises in steps, and the smooth curve is the version in which output is divisible.



Exit. Leaving the market permanently. The plant is sold and the lease ends, so the fixed costs stop too.



Two thresholds, two runs. In the short run the fixed cost is sunk, so the test compares the price with the minimum of \(AVC\). In the long run no future cost is fixed, because the firm can avoid every cost it has still to pay by leaving, so the test becomes the price against the minimum of \(ATC\).

Entry and exit. In the long run the number of firms is not fixed, and it is profit that changes it. A profit draws in entrants, which shifts market supply to the right and pushes the price down. A loss drives firms out, which shifts supply to the left and pushes the price up. In the short run a shift in demand moves the price. In the long run it moves the number of firms.



Long-run competitive equilibrium. The state in which \(P = MC\), so that each firm maximizes profit; \(P\) equals the minimum of \(ATC\), so that economic profit is zero and no firm enters or leaves; and each firm produces at its efficient scale.



Rent to a scarce advantage. A surplus earned by a firm whose costs are below those of the marginal entrant, because entrants cannot replicate the advantage that produces the lower costs. It survives in long-run equilibrium.



What makes long-run supply flat. The long-run supply curve is horizontal at the minimum of \(ATC\) when input prices are unaffected by the size of the industry and all firms have the same costs. Where input prices rise as the industry grows, or where each further entrant has higher costs than the one before it, the curve slopes upward, and the price settles at whatever covers the marginal entrant’s costs.

title: 12  Monopoly
text:
12.1 Definitions
The sensor firm is the sole maker of a specialized industrial sensor, and a patent protects it. It faces market demand \(P = 100 - 5Q\), so if it chooses \(Q = 4\) the demand curve answers \(P = 100 - 20 = 80\).
The sensor firm’s barrier is a government grant. Its patent gives it the exclusive right to sell, typically for 20 years.
The sensor firm earns $120 thousand a month. In a competitive market a profit of that size would draw entrants, but here the patent holds the door shut.
A city’s electricity grid costs \(TC = 160 + 10Q\), so \(ATC = 160/Q + 10\). Suppose 8,000 homes are to be served. One firm serving all of them has an average cost of $30 a home, while two firms serving 4,000 each have $50, because each pays the $160 thousand fixed cost for its own poles and wires.
To sell 8 thousand sensors rather than 7 thousand, the firm cuts the price from $65 to $60. The output effect is \(+60\) and the price effect is \(7 \times (-5) = -35\), so marginal revenue is only 25.
For the sensor firm, with \(TC = 200 + 20Q\), \(\pi = (60 - 45) \times 8 = 120\) (Figure 12.1). If the license fee doubled the fixed cost to 400, \(ATC\) at 8 would be 70, the rectangle would sit above the price line, and \(\pi = (60 - 70) \times 8 = -80\).
A competitive sensor market would sell 16 thousand at $20, and the monopolist sells 8 thousand at $60. Of the $640 thousand of surplus, $320 thousand is transferred to the firm and $160 thousand is destroyed (Figure 12.2).
At its single price of $60, the sensor firm lets the buyers of the second thousand, whose sensors were worth $90 to them, keep $30 each. It also excludes units 9 through 16, worth from $55 down to $20, that would be profitable to serve at a lower price.
If the city distributor, facing \(P = 70 - 5Q\), is capped at its marginal cost of $10, it connects all 12 thousand homes worth connecting but loses its whole fixed cost of $160 thousand a month. Capping it at average cost lets the firm break even at $30 and leaves homes 8,000 to 12,000 unserved (Figure 12.3).

title: 12  Monopoly
text:
Monopoly. A firm that is the sole seller of a product for which there are no close substitutes.



How a monopoly arises. There are three kinds of barrier. A key resource held in one firm’s hands, for example control of the essential input. A government grant, such as a patent, a copyright or a license, where the law itself keeps rivals out. A natural monopoly, where one firm can serve the whole market more cheaply than two firms could. In that case the cost structure itself does the excluding.



Barriers to entry. In a competitive market, profit attracted new entrants, and the entrants competed it away. A monopoly persists only because something blocks the door. If there is no barrier, there is no monopoly. Free entry always wears market power down.



Natural monopoly. An industry in which a single firm can supply the whole market at a lower average cost than two or more firms could.



Why marginal revenue falls short of the price. To sell more, the firm must let the price fall. The lower price applies to every unit, including those it was already selling, rather than only to the new one. So \(MR < P\) for any firm that faces a downward-sloping demand curve, and the gap between them is the price effect. A competitive firm escapes the price effect because its demand curve is flat, so \(MR = P\).



The profit rectangle, and how to build it. Start at the point where marginal revenue meets marginal cost, which fixes \(Q_{m}\). Climb straight up to the demand curve to get \(P_{m}\). Then drop down to the \(ATC\) curve at the same quantity. The gap is profit per unit. The profit rectangle runs from zero to \(Q_{m}\), with its top at the price and its bottom at \(ATC\).



Monopoly compared with perfect competition. The efficient quantity is found by making every unit whose value covers its cost, and stopping where value falls to cost. Competition pushes the price down to marginal cost. The monopolist is a case of trading too little. The deadweight loss triangle sits between the marginal cost line and the demand curve, and spans the quantities from \(Q_{m}\) to \(Q^{*}\). The profit is a transfer and the triangle is the loss. A monopoly price works like a private tax. It drives a wedge between what buyers pay and what production costs. The difference is that the revenue goes to the firm, rather than to a treasury.



Price discrimination. Selling the same good to different buyers at different prices, when it costs the same to serve each buyer.



Regulating a natural monopoly. For a natural monopoly of this kind, average total cost is above marginal cost everywhere. So a price equal to marginal cost is necessarily below average cost, and a price that covers average cost is necessarily above marginal cost. With a single price per unit, only a subsidy avoids the choice.

title: 13  Oligopoly
text:
13.1 Definitions
Consider a valley town with exactly two ready-mix concrete plants, Ridge Concrete and Vale Concrete, selling an identical product. Market demand is \(P = 60 - Q\), with \(Q\) in yards a day, and each plant produces at a marginal cost of $12 a yard, so each plant’s profit is \((P - 12)\) times the yards it sells.
Suppose Ridge produces \(q\) while Vale produces 12. The price is then \(60 - (12 + q) = 48 - q\), so Ridge’s profit,
\[
(48 - q - 12)\,q = (36 - q)\,q ,
\tag{13.1}\]
depends on Vale’s output as well as its own.
If a town’s six grocery stores have market shares of 30, 25, 20, 10, 10 and 5 percent, the four largest supply \(30 + 25 + 20 + 10 = 85\) percent. A market of ten firms with 10 percent each has a ratio of only 40 percent.
If Ridge and Vale collude, they produce the monopoly quantity of 24 yards between them, 12 each, at \(P = 60 - 24 = 36\). Each plant earns \((36 - 12) \times 12 = 288\), and joint profit is 576.
The cartel at 12 and 12 is not a Nash equilibrium, because a plant that deviates to 18 earns 324 against 288. The pair at 16 and 16 is one, since against a rival at 16 every deviation earns less than 256.
When Ridge and Vale choose quantities, they settle at 32 yards and $28, and each earns 256. When they post prices instead, they undercut each other down to $12, where the market takes 48 yards and each earns zero.
Mr Red and Mr Blue are questioned in separate rooms, and each may stay silent or confess. The payoffs are years in jail: one year each if both stay silent, two each if both confess, and zero for the one who confesses while the other stays silent and serves three.
Two food trucks each choose whether to keep their prices or to discount. If the rival keeps, a truck earns 650 by discounting against 500 by keeping, and if the rival discounts, it earns 400 against 300, so discounting is dominant.
Two streaming services that each choose a big advertising campaign end up with 80 each, although small campaigns would have given both of them 100.
Suppose Vale plays the grim strategy, mixing 16 forever once Ridge exceeds its quota. Cheating gains Ridge \(324 - 288 = 36\) once and costs it \(288 - 256 = 32\) in every later round, so if the plants expect to meet even twice more, \(36 < 32 + 32\) and cheating is a losing move.
If Ridge and Vale agreed on output, that would be naked price fixing, illegal in itself. It would move the market from 32 yards at $28 toward 24 yards at $36.

title: 13  Oligopoly
text:
Oligopoly. A market structure in which only a few sellers offer similar or identical products.



Strategic interdependence. Each firm’s best choice depends on the choices the other firms make, and every firm knows it.





Concentration ratio. The percentage of a market’s total output supplied by its four largest firms.



Collusion and cartels. Collusion is an agreement among firms in a market about the quantities to produce or the prices to charge. A cartel is a group of firms acting in unison.



Nash equilibrium. A situation in which each economic actor, interacting with others, chooses their best strategy given the strategies all the other actors have chosen.



What the firms compete over. The same two plants, with the same demand curve and the same marginal cost, produce either the competitive outcome or one well above it. Which one depends only on what the firms choose to compete over, and neither outcome involves an agreement.



Game. A strategic situation described by three lists: the players, the strategies each may choose, and the payoff each receives for every combination of choices.



Dominant strategy. A strategy that is best for a player no matter what strategy the other players choose.



Individual and collective rationality. Mutual silence gives one year each, which is better for Red and better for Blue than the two years each that rational play produces. So there is an outcome that is strictly better for both players at the same time, and rational play does not reach it. Individual rationality does not imply collective rationality.



Repeated game. The same game, played by the same players, round after round, with each round’s choices visible before the next.



The Sherman and Clayton Acts. The Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890 declares illegal every contract, combination or conspiracy in restraint of trade. It makes it a crime to monopolize or attempt to monopolize, and it lets a private party injured by a violation sue for three times its losses. The Clayton Act of 1914 carries those treble damages forward and adds private injunctive relief, under which courts may order conduct stopped.

title: 14  Monopolistic Competition
text:
14.1 Definitions
Consider a coffee roaster in a city of two hundred roasters, each with its own blend, its own shop and its own customers. Its output \(q\) is measured in thousands of pounds a year, its price \(P\) in dollars a pound, and its total cost is \(TC = 144 + 10q + q^{2}\) in thousands of dollars a year.
The roaster faces its own demand curve \(P = A - 3q\), so to sell one thousand pounds more it has to cut its price by $3. A price taker would need no price cut at all.
With demand at \(P = 74 - 3q\), so that \(MR = 74 - 6q\), and \(MC = 10 + 2q\), the roaster produces \(q = 8\) at a price of 50, its average total cost is 36, and its profit is \((50 - 36) \times 8 = 112\). With demand at \(P = 42 - 3q\) the same steps give \(q = 4\), a price of 30 and average total cost of 50, so it loses \((30 - 50) \times 4 = -80\).
Entry moves the roaster’s intercept from 74 down to 58, a fall of $16 at every quantity. At six units it could charge \(74 - 18 = 56\) before entry and only \(58 - 18 = 40\) after it.
In the long run the roaster produces 6 thousand pounds a year, and its efficient scale is 12, so its excess capacity is \(12 - 6 = 6\). Its average total cost is 40 where it could be 34.
At its long-run position the roaster charges 40 and its last unit costs 22, so the markup is \(40 - 22 = 18\) dollars a pound. A price-taking firm with the same costs charges 34 for a last unit that costs 34, a markup of nothing.
With the roaster’s costs, perfect competition gives a quantity of 12 at a price of 34, and monopolistic competition gives 6 at a price of 40. Profit is zero in both, which is why the differences between them are not about profit.
A firm whose customer is worth $60 over all the repeat purchases will pay $20 to win one. A firm whose customer is worth $6 will not, so the campaign itself tells the buyer which kind of firm is selling.
A customer who values a new roaster’s blend at $70 pays 40 like everyone else and keeps 30 of surplus. None of that 30 is the entrant’s revenue, so it plays no part in the decision to open.
A new roaster spends the fixed 144 to open, and some of its sales are the same customers buying from a different shop. That part of its profit is not new output but a loss to the roasters it has never met.

title: 14  Monopolistic Competition
text:
Monopolistic competition. A market in which there are many sellers, the products are differentiated, and firms are free to enter and exit.



What makes the demand curve slope down. The firm’s demand curve slopes down because its product is distinguishable from the others, not because it is the only seller. If a firm raises its price above every rival’s, it loses some of its customers rather than all of them. The ones who stay are those who preferred this seller by more than the amount of the price rise.



Four steps, in this order. First, set marginal revenue equal to marginal cost and solve for the quantity. Second, take that quantity up to the demand curve to find the price. Third, take the same quantity up to average total cost to find the cost per unit. Finally, profit is price minus average total cost, multiplied by the quantity.



Entry and exit move the firm’s own demand curve. Fewer customers at every price means the demand curve has shifted left. Read the other way, the firm must now charge less to sell any given quantity. Losses run the same mechanism backwards. When a roaster closes, its customers still want coffee, and they spread themselves among the shops that remain. So every surviving firm has more customers at any given price, and that pushes the intercept back up. The cost function does not move, whether firms are entering or leaving.



Excess capacity. The gap between the output a firm produces and its efficient scale.



The markup. Price minus marginal cost.



Against perfect competition and monopoly. Monopolistic competition shares free entry with perfect competition, along with its consequence, zero economic profit in the long run. It shares a downward-sloping demand curve with monopoly, along with its consequences: marginal revenue below price, and therefore a price above marginal cost.



Advertising as a signal. The content of an advertisement may say nothing useful, and yet the willingness to spend on it can still be informative. Advertising separates good firms from poor ones when the customers it wins come back. A firm that expects repeat purchases can recoup a cost that a firm selling something poor, which makes just one sale, cannot.



The product-variety externality. When a new firm enters with a product of its own, the consumers who prefer that product gain surplus that the entrant does not collect. The entrant charges one price, so buyers who would have paid far more for this particular blend keep the difference.



The business-stealing externality. When a new firm enters, it takes customers from firms already in the market, and their loss plays no part in its calculation.

title: 15  Consumer Choice
text:
15.1 Definitions
The buyer in this chapter has $120 a week to spend and faces \(p_y = \$2\) and \(p_x = \$3\). The bundle \((20,30)\) means 20 units of \(x\) and 30 units of \(y\).
By more is better, the buyer prefers \((40,60)\) to \((20,30)\), because it has more of both goods. Nothing in the list says the buyer is selfish, well informed or sensible.
With \(U(x,y) = \sqrt{xy}\), the bundle \((20,30)\) scores \(\sqrt{600} \approx 24.5\) and \((10,30)\) scores \(\sqrt{300} \approx 17.3\). All that tells us is that the buyer prefers the first. It does not say the first is 1.4 times as good.
Through \((20,30)\) the constant is \(k = 20 \times 30 = 600\). So \((10,60)\) and \((60,10)\) lie on the same curve, \(y = 600/x\), and the buyer is indifferent among all three bundles.
Moving along \(y = 600/x\) from \((10,60)\) to \((20,30)\), the buyer gives up 30 units of \(y\) for 10 of \(x\), an average of 3 per unit. From \((20,30)\) to \((40,15)\) the rate is only \(15/20 = 0.75\), so the rate falls as \(x\) rises.
Here the constraint is \(3x + 2y = 120\), or \(y = 60 - 1.5x\). The bundle \((16,36)\) exhausts the income exactly, since \(48 + 72 = 120\).
If \(x\) cost $6 instead, the ratio would be \(6/2 = 3\), and each unit of \(x\) would cost 3 units of \(y\). The line would be steeper.
At \((10,45)\) the buyer’s rate is \(45/10 = 4.5\) against the market’s 1.5, so at the margin \(x\) is worth more than it costs and the buyer buys more of it. At \((20,30)\) the condition reads \(30/20 = 1.5\) against \(3/2 = 1.5\), so it holds exactly.
With \(y = 30\), the marginal utility of \(x\) falls from 0.866 at \(x = 10\) to 0.612 at \(x = 20\), and to 0.433 at \(x = 40\).
At \((20,30)\), \(MU_x/p_x = 0.6124/3 = 0.2041\) and \(MU_y/p_y = 0.4082/2 = 0.2041\). Dividing one condition by the other gives \(y/x = p_x/p_y\), and putting that into the budget gives the chosen bundle,
\[
x^{*} = \frac{m}{2p_x} ,
  \qquad
  y^{*} = \frac{m}{2p_y} .
\tag{15.1}\]
With \(m = 120\), Equation (15.1) gives \(x^{*} = 60/p_x\). Spending on \(x\) is then \(p_x x^{*} = \$60\) whatever the price, so half the budget always goes on each good.
With $180 and \(p_x = \$6\), the buyer chooses \(C = (15,45)\), since \(180/12 = 15\) and \(180/4 = 45\).
When \(p_x\) doubles from $3 to $6, the buyer moves from \(A = (20,30)\) to \(B = (10,30)\). The substitution effect takes \(x\) from 20 to 15 and the income effect from 15 to 10, so each is \(-5\) and together they make \(-10\).
Under the compensated income of $180, bundle \(A\) costs \(6(20) + 2(30) = 180\), so it was affordable, and yet the buyer chose \(C\). So \(C\) is at least as good as \(A\).
Such goods are rare. The clearest evidence is the finding of Jensen and Miller (2008) for rice among very poor households in China.

title: 15  Consumer Choice
text:
Bundle. A list of quantities, so much of one good and so much of another. When there are two goods, it is just a pair of numbers, \((x, y)\).



The three assumptions. More is better: a bundle that has more of both goods is preferred. Completeness: any two bundles can be compared with each other. Consistency: if \(A\) is preferred to \(B\) and \(B\) is preferred to \(C\), then \(A\) is preferred to \(C\).



Utility. A number attached to a bundle, arranged so that a preferred bundle gets a higher number. Only the ordering of those numbers carries meaning.



Indifference curve. The set of bundles among which the buyer is indifferent, with every point on it delivering the same utility. For this function it is the graph of \(y = k/x\), which is a rectangular hyperbola. To find the curve through a particular bundle, multiply its two coordinates together.



Marginal rate of substitution. The amount of \(y\) that the buyer will give up for one more unit of \(x\), with utility held constant. It is the slope of the indifference curve without its minus sign, and we write it as \(MRS\).



The budget constraint. With two goods, prices \(p_x\) and \(p_y\) and income \(m\), the bundles that exhaust income are the ones that satisfy \(p_x x + p_y y = m\). Every coefficient is a price, and the right-hand side is income. So nothing in the equation refers to taste.



The slope is a rate of exchange between goods. The size of the slope, 1.5, is not an amount of money. Three dollars buys one unit of \(x\), and three dollars also buys one and a half units of \(y\). So the price of \(x\), measured in units of \(y\), is 1.5. To get one more unit of \(x\), the market requires the buyer to give up 1.5 units of \(y\).



The tangency condition. The only bundle from which the buyer wants no move is the one where the buyer’s rate and the market’s rate coincide: \[MRS = \frac{p_x}{p_y} ,
  \qquad\text{which here reads}\qquad
  \frac{y}{x} = \frac{p_x}{p_y} .\] For a line to be tangent to a curve means that they have equal slopes at a shared point. So the optimum is a tangency.



Marginal utility. The extra utility from one more unit of a good, holding the other good fixed. Mathematically, it is a partial derivative. For \(U = x^{1/2}y^{1/2}\), \[MU_x = \frac{\partial U}{\partial x} = \tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{y}{x}} ,
  \qquad
  MU_y = \frac{\partial U}{\partial y} = \tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{x}{y}} .\]



Equal marginal utility per dollar. At the optimum \[\frac{MU_x}{p_x} = \mu = \frac{MU_y}{p_y} ,\] so the last dollar spent on each good buys the same amount of utility.




A demand function. A rule that maps each price to the quantity a buyer chooses when doing the best that is available at that price. In effect it is a solved maximization problem, with one answer for each price.



Slutsky compensation. Enough income is given to the buyer for the original bundle to be affordable at the new prices. Costing \(A = (20,30)\) at the new prices gives \[m' = p_x^{\text{new}}x_A + p_y y_A = 6(20) + 2(30) = 120 + 60 = \$180 ,\] which is $60 more than the buyer had before.



Income and substitution effects. When the price of \(x\) rises, the good becomes dearer relative to \(y\), and the buyer also becomes poorer. The substitution effect is the move from \(A\) to \(C\), which changes the relative price while purchasing power is held fixed. The income effect is the move from \(C\) to \(B\), which takes the compensation away, with prices unchanged.



Revealed preference. If a bundle is chosen when another bundle was affordable, the chosen bundle is at least as good as the other. No utility function need exist for the principle to apply. It concerns choices and prices alone.



Giffen good. A good whose ordinary demand curve slopes upward. This happens when the income effect is positive and large enough to outweigh the substitution effect.
